analysis.title: AI on the factory floor: Assessing the opportunity in physical AI
key_insights: Mizuho says physical AI (intelligence embedded in machines that sense, reason and act) is already affecting operations on factory floors, with uptake showing few signs of slowing.

Structured industrial environments with repeatable processes and measurable outcomes make physical AI easier to train, test and scale. Most industrial equipment already has sensors, chips and software, so companies can layer AI onto existing robots, controls, valves and pumps without rebuilding a factory.

Mizuho expects the earliest deployments to be practical rather than humanoid robots: AI-enabled inspections, predictive maintenance and semi-structured material handling, where safety stakes are lower, redesign needs are modest and benefits are measurable.
Mentions of 'physical AI' on earnings calls and at industry events rose from 92 in Q1 2024 to 975 in Q1 2026, a more than 10x increase in two years.
Robotics and physical AI startups raised $16.3 billion across 492 deals in Q1 2026, a record quarter by both measures. Trailing 12-month deal value approached $40 billion.
Physical AI and robotics was not a category among the top 100 US private companies in 2016. By 2026 it reached $263 billion in total value, second only to AI and software.

Mizuho sees two layers of opportunity. The automation layer covers companies that build and integrate industrial machines and systems and also use them internally. The component supply chain layer covers bearings, actuators, sensors, servomotors, drives, connectors and thermal management.
In the automation layer, Mizuho favors names with large installed bases, embedded software and proprietary data. Names with primarily commoditized hardware are seen as more challenged.

Mizuho says the component opportunity is underappreciated for some companies because it is embedded in existing product lines. It cites order books and capex plans as evidence that physical AI is becoming commercially viable before it fully matures.

Mizuho calls physical AI an early-cycle story. Challenges include compute and power availability, grid interconnections and supply-chain constraints, which it views as generally manageable. It calls internal productivity the most investable near-term lever.

sector_views.rationale: Mizuho sees physical AI as a differentiated avenue into the larger AI story. It favors automation-layer companies with large installed bases, embedded software and proprietary data, and component suppliers whose physical AI exposure is embedded in existing product lines.

earnings_insights: Mentions of 'physical AI' on earnings calls and at industry events reached 975 in Q1 2026 versus 92 in Q1 2024, per Mizuho's data.
